title: Oil Crashes to Pre-War Levels as Saudi Exports Resume — and India Gets a $40-a-Barrel Windfall
excerpt: Brent crude plunged 11% in a week to $72 as tankers flooded through the Strait of Hormuz, handing India's economy its best macro news in four months.
body:
Crude oil prices have crashed to their lowest level since before the Iran war began on February 28, erasing nearly four months of a geopolitical risk premium in the space of a single week — and India, the world's third-largest oil importer, stands to benefit more than almost any other major economy.

Brent crude settled at **$71.99 a barrel on Friday**, down 10.86 per cent for the week and more than $40 below its wartime peak of $126.41 in April. West Texas Intermediate fell 9.62 per cent to $69.23. It was the steepest weekly decline since the Strait of Hormuz crisis began.

## What Changed

The immediate catalyst was the accelerating flow of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz following the 60-day ceasefire between the United States and Iran. Tanker traffic through the strait hit a single-day record of roughly 16 million barrels earlier in the week, surpassing even pre-war volumes. On Friday, Saudi Aramco resumed oil loading at its Ras Tanura terminal in the Persian Gulf after a nearly four-month halt — a symbolic and practical milestone.

"There is a growing sense that oil is going to keep moving through the Strait of Hormuz," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. "I think we're going to see a huge flood of products."

The structural signal was louder still. Brent's prompt spread flipped into **contango** — where near-term prices fall below future contracts — for the first time since the conflict began. In market language, that is the clearest signal that near-term supply is no longer scarce.


![Saudi Aramco — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/Aramco_Tower.jpg)



> **""There is a growing sense that oil is going to keep moving through the Strait of Hormuz," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group."**



## India's Triple Dividend

For India, this is unambiguously good news. The country imports over 85 per cent of its crude oil needs, and every dollar drop in Brent saves roughly $1.5 billion on the annual import bill.

**First, inflation relief.** Energy costs were a primary driver of the spike in India's consumer price inflation during the war months. Petrol and diesel prices at Indian pumps, which were raised twice during the crisis, may now face downward pressure. The Reserve Bank of India's governor, Sanjay Malhotra, said this week it was "premature to discuss rate hikes," noting the central bank did not yet see signs of inflation becoming broad-based.

**Second, the current account.** India's current account deficit ballooned during the war as oil imports surged in price. A sustained return to $70-75 Brent would narrow the deficit materially, reducing pressure on the rupee and strengthening the macro story for foreign investors.

**Third, markets.** Indian equities posted their third consecutive weekly gain, the longest winning streak in seven months. The Nifty 50 rose to 24,056 and the Sensex to 77,100. Six of 16 major sectors advanced, with pharma stocks the standout after reports that the US FDA reached out to Indian drugmakers for a critical cancer drug.

## The Cautious Case


![Persian Gulf — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg/3840px-PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg)


The IMF, however, warned that normalization will take time. Spokesperson Julie Kozack said that while energy prices have fallen, "there will be some time before we go back to a normal state, and of course that all assumes that the ceasefire remains in place."

Risks remain. Iran's Revolutionary Guard attacked a Singapore-flagged cargo vessel near Oman even as tankers were transiting the strait, prompting the International Maritime Organization to briefly pause evacuation operations. The ceasefire is 60 days old, not permanent.

And demand is softer than the supply surge suggests. Asian refiners are slowing their Middle East crude purchases, and China has not yet picked up crude demand — a sign that even cheaper oil is not pulling buying forward the way it normally would.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For diaspora investors with India-linked portfolios, the oil crash resets a key input in the India equity thesis. Lower oil strengthens the rupee, improves corporate margins for oil-dependent sectors (airlines, logistics, paint, chemicals), and gives the RBI room to keep rates accommodative.

The caveat: oil stocks and refinery margins cut the other way. ONGC, Oil India and IOC — popular dividend plays among NRI investors — could see earnings pressure at $70 Brent.

As PVM analyst Tamas Varga put it: "The predominant view, it appears, remains one of imminent oversupply." For India, that is the best macroeconomic news in four months.

*Sources: Reuters; Wall Street Journal; FXStreet; IMF Press Briefing (June 26, 2026)*
